title: Pain assessment and management
blurb: Assess pain with the right tool (including when people cannot tell you), relieve it, reassess and escalate.
question: Mr O'Neill, 87, has advanced dementia and a fractured wrist. He cannot rate his pain, but he grimaces, groans and pulls his arm away when his sleeve is touched. How should the nurse assess his pain?

teach.h: Pain is what the person says it is
teach.body: Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience, and only the person feels it. UK national guidelines on assessing pain in older people state that self-report is the most valid and reliable indicator of pain. In plain English: ask, believe and record what the person tells you. When someone cannot tell you (advanced dementia, some learning disabilities, sedation, a ventilator), watch their behaviour with a validated tool instead.
teach.cite: Assessment of pain in older people: UK national guidelines (BGS/BPS, Age and Ageing 2018)

children.label: Numerical rating 0–10
children.sub: Or verbal descriptors: none, mild, moderate, severe

children.label: Simple self-report
children.sub: Verbal descriptors often work; ask in different ways

teach.caption: UK national guidelines on pain in older people (2018) recommend PAINAD or Doloplus-2 when severe cognitive impairment prevents self-report; the Abbey Pain Scale is also widely used in the UK. NICE NG31 rec 1.5.14 asks for a validated behavioural assessment for people in the last days of life who cannot explain their pain.

head: Domain
What you might see
rows: Agitation, refusing care, withdrawal, hitting out
Rising pulse or BP, sweating, pallor
Off food, poor sleep, change in mobility
teach.caption: NICE CG103 rec 1.4.9: look for non-verbal signs of pain, particularly in people with communication difficulties.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr O'Neill on the orthopaedic ward
teach.body: Mr O'Neill cannot use a number scale, so the nurse uses a behavioural tool such as PAINAD while he is moved, records the score, and asks his daughter what is normal for him. She gives his prescribed analgesia, supports the wrist on a pillow and reassesses with the same tool once the medicine should be working. Because his behaviour improves, the plan continues; if it had not, she would have escalated to the prescriber.

teach.caption: Use the same tool each time so scores are comparable. Treat reversible causes (for example urinary retention or constipation) as well as the pain.
NICE NG31 recs 1.5.10 and 1.5.13 (last days of life): consider non-pharmacological methods and match the medicine to the severity of pain. The same principles apply at other times.

steps.label: Constipation
steps.sub: Expect it; plan a laxative (osmotic or stimulant)

steps.label: Drowsiness
steps.sub: Check sedation with each observation set

steps.label: Act
steps.sub: Stop the opioid, support breathing, call for help, naloxone if trained

teach.caption: CKS (2026): bulk-forming laxatives are not used for opioid-induced constipation. RCUK 2025: give naloxone for suspected opioid overdose if trained.

teach.body: Unrelieved pain slows recovery, disturbs sleep, reduces mobility and can trigger delirium. NICE safe staffing guidance (SG1) lists a delay of more than 30 minutes in giving pain relief as a nursing red flag event. Believe the person's report, give prescribed analgesia promptly, and do not let assumptions about 'drug seeking' or stoicism delay care (Code 1.3, 1.4).

teach.text: A calm face does not mean no pain, and a high score does not mean exaggeration. Self-report wins when the person can give it. And always reassess after giving analgesia: recording a score only before treatment tells you nothing about whether it worked.

items: Self-report is the most valid indicator of pain; numerical or verbal scales if the person can use them.
Cannot self-report: behavioural tool; the UK pain in older people guidelines (2018) recommend PAINAD or Doloplus-2, and Abbey is widely used.
Assess, relieve, reassess with the same tool, record, escalate if not controlled.
Look for reversible causes, such as urinary retention or constipation.
Opioids: plan for constipation; watch for drowsiness and slow breathing; naloxone if toxicity.

summary: You can now choose a pain assessment tool that fits the person, including behavioural tools for those who cannot self-report, and run the assess, relieve, reassess cycle. You can also anticipate opioid side effects and recognise toxicity that needs urgent action.

A.q: Mrs Grant, 54, is two hours after a hysterectomy and rates her pain at 8 out of 10. She was given prescribed oral morphine 40 minutes ago. What should the nurse do now?
options: Give a further dose of morphine straight away
Reassess her pain and record the effect of the dose
Record the score of 8 and check her again at 4 hours
Tell her the morphine needs longer to work fully
A.why: After analgesia, reassess using the same tool and record the effect; if pain is still severe, escalate or give further prescribed analgesia as appropriate.

whyNot.0: A further dose without reassessment and within the prescribed interval could cause toxicity.
whyNot.2: Waiting 4 hours leaves severe pain unmanaged and unreviewed.
whyNot.3: Dismissing her report without reassessing delays relief.

A.q: Mr Patel, 90, has severe dementia and cannot describe his pain. After a fall he grimaces and guards his left hip when moved. Which assessment is most appropriate?
options: A numerical rating scale from 0 to 10
Asking him to point to a faces chart
A behavioural pain tool such as PAINAD
His pulse and blood pressure as a proxy
A.why: UK national guidelines on assessing pain in older people (2018) recommend behavioural tools such as PAINAD or Doloplus-2 for people with severe cognitive impairment who cannot self-report; the Abbey Pain Scale is also widely used in the UK.

whyNot.0: A 0–10 scale needs abstract thinking he cannot manage with severe dementia.
whyNot.1: A faces chart is still self-report, which he cannot reliably give.
whyNot.3: Vital signs can change with pain but are not a validated pain measure on their own.

A.q: Mr Haddad, 61, has been taking regular codeine for back pain for a week. Which side effect should the nurse ask about and plan to prevent?
options: Diarrhoea
Insomnia
Hypertension
Constipation
A.why: Opioids such as codeine commonly cause constipation; plan prevention (CKS: an osmotic or stimulant laxative, not a bulk-forming one).

whyNot.0: Opioids slow the gut, so diarrhoea is not the expected effect.
whyNot.1: Opioids more often cause drowsiness than insomnia.
whyNot.2: Opioids are not known for raising blood pressure.

B.q: Mr Lewis, 66, has a morphine PCA after bowel surgery. He is difficult to rouse, breathing 7 times a minute, with pinpoint pupils. His wife has been pressing the button for him. What is the priority?
options: Remove the handset so that his wife cannot use it again
Encourage him to take deep breaths and recheck in 15 minutes
Record the observations and inform the pain team in the morning
Stop the PCA, support his breathing and call for urgent help
B.why: These are signs of opioid toxicity. Stop the opioid, support airway and breathing, call for urgent help and give naloxone as prescribed or per protocol (RCUK 2025 opioid poisoning).

whyNot.0: Removing the handset alone leaves the toxicity untreated.
whyNot.1: A respiratory rate of 7 needs immediate support, not encouragement and a wait.

B.q: Ruth, 28, has sickle cell disease and arrives with severe pain. A colleague says she is 'drug seeking' because she asks for morphine by name. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept her report and give prescribed analgesia promptly
Give paracetamol first to see whether the pain is genuine
Ask her to wait until her observations show signs of pain
Withhold opioids until the medical team has reviewed her
B.why: Self-report is the most valid indicator of pain. Delays in pain relief are a safety red flag (NICE SG1), and assumptions breach Code 1.3.

whyNot.1: Testing whether pain is 'genuine' disbelieves her and delays effective relief.
whyNot.2: Vital signs may stay normal in severe pain; self-report takes priority.
whyNot.3: If analgesia is prescribed, withholding it delays care without reason.

B.q: Joan, 74, has back pain after a fall and is on a frailty unit. Which non-drug measure is most likely to help alongside her prescribed analgesia?
options: Strict bed rest until the pain fully settles
Repositioning using pillows for support
Massage over her bony prominences
Restricting fluids to reduce toilet trips
B.why: Repositioning with pillows for support is a simple non-pharmacological comfort measure that works alongside prescribed analgesia without adding risk.

whyNot.0: Strict bed rest increases pressure ulcer and VTE risk and causes deconditioning that raises falls risk; she should keep moving within her comfort.
whyNot.2: NICE CG179 advises against massaging or rubbing skin to prevent pressure ulcers.
whyNot.3: Restricting fluids risks dehydration and constipation.

C.q: Mrs Dunn, 89, has a hip fracture and regular analgesia. At 02:00 she is restless and calling out. Her PAINAD score is 7 and she has not passed urine for 9 hours. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask for p.r.n. sedation to help her settle for the night
Give her next analgesia dose early and recheck at 06:00
Assess for urinary retention and escalate to the doctor
Raise the bed rails and move her closer to the station
C.why: A high behavioural pain score with no urine for 9 hours suggests urinary retention as a reversible cause of pain and agitation. Assess (bladder scan) and escalate to the doctor.

whyNot.0: Sedation hides the cause and increases falls and delirium risk.
whyNot.1: Giving a dose early without a prescription is unsafe and misses the likely cause.
whyNot.3: Bed rails need a risk assessment and do not address her pain.

C.q: Mr Ito, 72, uses the 0–10 scale. Before analgesia he scores 9; one hour after IV morphine he scores 8 and is alert with a respiratory rate of 16. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Document the small improvement and continue the current plan
Escalate to the prescriber as his pain is poorly controlled
Switch to a behavioural tool as his score has hardly changed
Tell him a score of 8 is acceptable after his type of surgery
C.why: Reassessment shows pain is still severe with no sedation, so the plan needs review: escalate to the prescriber (Code 13.2: make a timely referral when action or treatment is required).

whyNot.0: A drop from 9 to 8 is not adequate control; continuing unchanged leaves him in pain.
whyNot.2: He can self-report, which is more valid than a behavioural tool.
whyNot.3: Deciding what pain is acceptable for him overrides his own report.

C.q: Mr Barnes, 68, takes regular morphine for cancer pain and has not opened his bowels for 4 days. Which laxative approach is consistent with current CKS guidance for opioid-induced constipation?
options: A bulk-forming laxative such as ispaghula husk
Increasing his fluid intake as the first-line treatment
An osmotic or a stimulant laxative as prescribed
Stopping the morphine until his bowels have opened
C.why: CKS (revised July 2026): for opioid-induced constipation do not use bulk-forming laxatives; offer an osmotic or stimulant laxative.

whyNot.0: CKS advises against bulk-forming laxatives for opioid-induced constipation; an osmotic or stimulant laxative is used instead.
whyNot.1: Extra fluid alone does not treat constipation in people who are not dehydrated.
whyNot.3: Stopping analgesia would leave his cancer pain uncontrolled.

reteach.title: Two routes to the same answer
reteach.question: If a person can tell you about their pain, ask. If they cannot, how else can you find out?

blocks.body: Route one is self-report: a number from 0 to 10 or words like mild, moderate and severe. It is the gold standard. Route two is observation with a validated behavioural tool, used when someone cannot report pain: you score face, voice, body language and behaviour, ideally while they move. Whichever route you use, use the same one every time so you can see change.

blocks.text: Do not switch to a behavioural tool just because someone is older or mildly confused: many people with mild to moderate cognitive impairment can still use a simple self-report scale.

explain.body: Self-report is the most valid and reliable indicator of pain. Use a 0–10 numerical scale or verbal descriptors; these can work even with mild to moderate cognitive impairment if you ask in different ways.

test.q: Which is the most valid indicator of pain in a person able to communicate?
options: Their heart rate
A relative's view
Their facial expression
Their self-report
test.why: UK national guidelines: self-report is the most valid and reliable indicator of pain.

whyNot.0: Heart rate changes for many reasons and is not a pain measure.
whyNot.1: A relative's view helps but does not replace the person's own report.
whyNot.2: Facial expression is used when self-report is not possible.

explain.body: For people who cannot explain their pain (for example advanced dementia or a learning disability), UK national guidelines on pain in older people (2018) recommend a validated behavioural tool such as PAINAD or Doloplus-2; Abbey is widely used in the UK. NICE NG31 rec 1.5.14 gives the same advice for people in the last days of life.

test.q: Ellie, 40, has a profound learning disability and cannot speak. Which approach to pain assessment is most appropriate?
options: A 0–10 numerical scale
Assume she is in pain if crying
A validated behavioural tool
A verbal descriptor scale
test.why: For a person who cannot explain that they are in pain, such as someone with a profound learning disability, use a validated behavioural pain assessment rather than a self-report scale.

whyNot.0: A numerical scale relies on self-report she cannot give.
whyNot.1: Crying is one sign, but a structured validated tool is needed.
whyNot.3: Verbal descriptors also rely on self-report.

explain.body: After any intervention, reassess with the same tool once the treatment should have worked, record the effect and escalate if pain is not controlled. Look for reversible causes such as urinary retention or constipation.

test.q: What should follow every dose of analgesia given for acute pain?
options: A planned reassessment
A fluid balance check
A routine bladder scan
A capillary glucose
test.why: Reassessing after analgesia shows whether it worked and whether to escalate.

whyNot.1: Fluid balance is unrelated to judging analgesic effect.
whyNot.2: A bladder scan is for suspected retention, not after every dose.
whyNot.3: Glucose is not part of routine analgesia review.

explain.body: Expect constipation and plan an osmotic or stimulant laxative (not bulk-forming). Watch sedation and breathing. Slow breathing, extreme drowsiness and pinpoint pupils suggest toxicity: stop the opioid, support breathing, call for help, naloxone if trained.

test.q: Which combination most strongly suggests opioid toxicity?
options: Fast pulse and widely dilated pupils
Slow breathing and pinpoint pupils
Fever and a new cough
Itching and a dry mouth
test.why: RCUK 2025: suspect opioid overdose with slow or irregular breathing, extreme drowsiness and very small pupils.

whyNot.0: Dilated pupils and tachycardia are not typical of opioid toxicity.
whyNot.3: Itching and dry mouth are side effects, not signs of toxicity.
